findings.situation: A filer who is in the trade or business of gambling would truthfully enter all gambling losses, including those already deducted on Schedule C, and line 16 would deduct them again on Schedule A.
findings.source_text: p525 p. 33: "If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040). For tax years 2018 through 2025, professional gambling losses and expenses are limited to the amount of your winnings."; question: "Your gambling losses during 2025 ... in full"
findings.why: Neither the question nor its help excludes professional gambling losses that are reported on Schedule C. Those losses would be counted twice, once on Schedule C and again on Schedule A line 16.

findings.situation: A filer paid medical bills for a parent they supported but could not claim as a dependent only because the filer (or the filer's spouse, on a joint return) can be claimed as a dependent on someone else's 2025 return; the question's list of people does not include that parent, so the filer leaves those bills out.
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 2, Whose medical and dental expenses can you include: "Any person you could have claimed as a dependent except that you or your spouse if filing jointly can be claimed as a dependent on someone else's 2025 return."
findings.why: The question's list stops at the gross-income and joint-return exceptions and leaves out this fifth category, so expenses that line 1 needs are not included.

findings.situation: A filer whose cash gifts exceed the AGI-based limit (e.g., more than 30% or 60% of Form 1040 line 11b) enters the full pre-limit total, but line 11 needs only the deductible, limited amount.
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 10, Line 11: "Enter on line 11 the total value of gifts you made in cash or by check ... unless a limit on deducting gifts applies to you"; "Only enter on line 11 the deductible value of gifts you made in cash or by check." Question: "Deductible cash/check charitable gifts before income limits"
findings.why: Line 11 takes the amount after the income limits. The question explicitly asks for the amount before them, and nothing downstream applies the limit before the answer is used as line 11.

findings.situation: A filer who paid a charity and received a state or local tax credit, or who paid nondeductible items such as political contributions, raffle tickets, tuition, athletic-seating rights, club dues, or gifts to individuals, includes them because the help says only 'Charitable gifts by cash or check ... after subtracting benefits you received.'
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 10, Amounts You Can't Deduct: "Certain contributions to charitable organizations to the extent that you receive a state or local tax credit in return"; "An amount paid to or for the benefit of a college or university in exchange for the right to purchase tickets to an athletic event"; "Political contributions"; "Cost of raffle, bingo, or lottery tickets"; "Cost of tuition"
findings.why: The help names only the subtraction for benefits received. It does not exclude tax-credit-reduced amounts or the listed nondeductible payments, so a truthful answer can include amounts line 11 must not have.

findings.situation: A filer who made cash gifts with no bank record or written charity record, or a gift of $250 or more with no contemporaneous written acknowledgment, includes them because the help never mentions substantiation.
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 10, Recordkeeping: "For any contribution made in cash, regardless of the amount, you must maintain ... a bank record ... or a written record from the charity"; "For contributions of $250 or more, you must also have a contemporaneous written acknowledgment"
findings.why: The label says 'after ... required substantiation,' but the help shown does not tell the filer to leave out unsubstantiated gifts. A filer reading the help would include them.

findings.situation: A filer includes travel costs, such as meals and lodging away from home while volunteering, on a trip with a significant element of personal pleasure, because the help says to include 'out-of-pocket costs of volunteer work.'
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 10: "Travel expenses (including meals and lodging) while away from home performing donated services, unless there was no significant element of personal pleasure, recreation, or vacation in the travel."
findings.why: The help invites all out-of-pocket volunteer costs without this exclusion.

findings.situation: A filer who gave by credit/debit card or payroll deduction may read 'by cash or check' as excluding those gifts and report them elsewhere or omit them.
findings.source_text: Question help: "Charitable gifts by cash or check in 2025"; gate: "money given to a charity by cash, check, card or payroll deduction"; i1040sca p. 10: "a bank record (such as a canceled check or credit card statement)"; "If you made contributions through payroll deduction"
findings.why: Line 11 covers card and payroll-deduction gifts. The literal 'cash or check' wording can reasonably be read either way, which changes the amount entered.

findings.situation: A filer made a cash gift to a section 170(c) charity, received a state or local tax credit for it, and applied that credit against their 2025 real estate tax bill, so less real estate tax was paid out of pocket.
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 3: "If you meet these conditions and to the extent you apply the state or local tax credit to this or a prior year's state or local tax liability, you may include this amount on line 5a, 5b, or 5c, whichever is appropriate."
findings.why: The question and its help ask only for real estate taxes the filer paid and never mention this safe harbor. A filer answering truthfully would leave out the part of the tax satisfied by the credit, which the text allows on line 5b and line 5d needs.

findings.situation: A filer made a cash gift to a section 170(c) charity, received a state or local tax credit in return, and applied that credit against a value-based yearly personal property tax liability. The disallowed charitable amount is a payment that belongs on line 5c.
findings.source_text: i1040sca p. 3: "If you meet these conditions and to the extent you apply the state or local tax credit to this or a prior year's state or local tax liability, you may include this amount on line 5a, 5b, or 5c, whichever is appropriate."
findings.why: The question and its help ask only for personal property taxes the filer paid. A filer answering truthfully would leave out the charitable-contribution amount that the safe harbor treats as a payment of personal property tax, so line 5d would be too low.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1098 mortgage interest is subject to the debt or use limits (for example, mortgage debt above the limit, or a loan not used to buy, build, or improve the home) must still enter the limited, deductible portion on line 8a, but the question only asks for interest 'when no debt or use limit applies'.
findings.source_text: f1040sa 2025 p.1, line 8a: "Home mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098. See instructions if limited"; line 8: "If you didn't use all of your home mortgage loan(s) to buy, build, or improve your home, see instructions and check this box"
findings.why: Line 8a covers limited filers too; they enter the deductible amount figured under the instructions. The question excludes them, so a truthful limited filer gives zero or nothing, and line 8e loses their deductible Form 1098 interest. No gate or refusal is listed that sends these filers elsewhere.

findings.situation: A filer whose interest is limited reads 'after confirming the debt/use limits do not apply' together with 'Zero if none'. One reading is to enter zero. Another is to enter the full Form 1098 amount anyway. A third is to enter the limited amount.
findings.source_text: Question help: "Home mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098, when no debt or use limit applies. Zero if none." vs. f1040sa 2025 p.1, line 8a: "See instructions if limited"
findings.why: The wording does not say what to enter when a limit does apply. Reasonable filers would give different values: zero, the full amount, or the limited amount.

findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer's spouse was born in 1960, had no income, isn't filing and can't be claimed as a dependent, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65; the filer may answer yes, but the line must not allow the age box.
findings.source_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 33, Line 12d: "If your spouse was born before January 2, 1961, but died in 2025 before reaching age 65, don't check the box that says 'Spouse was born before January 2, 1961.'"
findings.why: The question asks "claiming age or blindness boxes for your spouse" but does not give the qualifying test or the death rule. A filer going by year of birth would answer yes when the spouse does not qualify.

findings.situation: A filer whose spouse turned 65 in 2026, or whose spouse has impaired vision but was not legally blind at the end of 2025, cannot tell from the wording or help whether the spouse qualifies for an 'age or blindness box'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 33, Line 12d: "your spouse was born before January 2, 1961, or was blind at the end of 2025"
findings.why: The question and help say only "age or blindness boxes". They omit the born-before-January 2, 1961 date and the end-of-2025 blindness test, so filers may apply different age or vision standards and give different answers.
